oil.summary: Crude markets are caught in a tug-of-war between recovering Persian Gulf supply and persistent Hormuz disruptions. WTI finished fractionally higher at $83.76 (+0.65%) but Brent shed 2.0% to $90.13, extending a punishing month that has erased more than 20% from the front-month contract. The dominant bear case is a rebuilding global glut: Chinese Persian Gulf imports surged 42.4% in October as the strait reopens, US inventories are rising, and a temporary US easing of Russian oil sanctions has added incremental supply—angering European allies and sparking bipartisan pushback in Congress. Offsetting factors include Iran's intensifying daily tanker attacks, a near-halving of Russian refinery output from Ukrainian strikes, and a Trump warning to Zelensky to halt those attacks. CME options now price a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the May 2027 meeting, underscoring how far sentiment has shifted bearish.
drivers: Supply glut fears dominate: recovering Gulf flows, rising US inventories, and temporary US relief on Russian oil sanctions overwhelm geopolitical risk premium
Iran escalating daily Hormuz tanker attacks while Persian Gulf crude flows simultaneously recover, creating an unusual divergence between physical disruption and price direction
OPEC cut probability hits 77% (CME options) as month-on-month price collapse of ~20% signals markets expect producers to respond

gas.summary: Henry Hub exploded higher, surging 15.5% on the day to $3.776/MMBtu and now up 35% on the month—the standout move across energy today. The backdrop is tightening supply after what has been characterised as the largest oil and gas disruption on record stemming from the Iran war. Europe is burning through storage fast—11% of summer injections drained in under a month heading into winter—while starting stocks were already low, pushing TTF up 5% on the day to €88.7/MWh despite a softer week. Norway is ramping hard, with October gas sales nearly 20% above year-ago levels, providing some relief on the European side. India's LPG demand rebounded to an eight-month high in October as supply recovered post-Hormuz shock. The Baker Hughes rig count for US oil and gas ticked higher this week, though the supply response will take time to materialise.
drivers: Henry Hub +15.5% on the day and +35% on the month as Iran-war supply shock continues to reverberate through global gas markets
European storage drawdown accelerating—11% of summer injections consumed in under a month—with winter demand just beginning; TTF +5% on the day
Norway gas sales +20% in October providing incremental supply relief; US rig count rising but physical response will lag

power.summary: The power and carbon desk has limited price-specific news flow today beyond TTF and EUA levels. EU carbon slipped 1.2% to $77.44/EUA and is down 7.8% on the week, likely pressured by the broader commodity selloff and near-term demand uncertainty. TTF's sharp daily rally (+5%) is a cost push for gas-fired generators but has not been enough to lift EUAs. On the structural side, a notable headline flags that Democratic governors will oversee states holding 77% of the 300 GW in US data centre capacity announced for 2027–2030, raising questions about permitting and grid-integration policy from January. A US-China-Russia superpower summit on the APEC sidelines delivered pledges around fuel supplies and nuclear dialogue but no concrete breakthroughs per reporting. The six-month mark of the Iran war is drawing formal CSIS analysis on energy and national security implications.
drivers: EU EUAs down 7.8% on the week, decoupling from a sharply higher TTF as bearish macro sentiment and weak near-term industrial demand weigh on carbon
US data centre power demand build-out (300 GW announced for 2027-2030) faces new political uncertainty as Democratic governors take control of key host states in January
Superpower summit (Trump-Xi-Putin) produced broad language on boosting fuel supplies and nuclear dialogue but no actionable policy detail
sources: CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies
